clue.text: Rate case of Chianti about standard

parts.note: to rate something is to class or grade it

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards
a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the wine

explanation.surface: A wine critic scores a case of Chianti against some benchmark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' could mean circa, giving C, but here it turns round only the wine's outer letters, which then follow the word for grading.
explanation.definitionFit: A classic is a standard work, the established model by which others are judged; both work as nouns.

clue.text: Rewrite clue as group of words containing a verb

definitions.text: group of words containing a verb

indicators.note: rewriting something sets it down again in a new form, so the letters come out rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grammar teacher's instruction to recast a crossword hint as a phrase with a verb in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The grammatical surface is self-referential: the definition is itself a textbook description, and the six letters of the two short words are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar a clause is a unit of language built around a finite verb, smaller than a full sentence.

clue.text: Flower delivery service

definitions.meaning: first meaning: something that flows, a river, here the great South American one
second meaning: the online retailer that delivers parcels

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a florist's delivery company; in crosswords 'flower' often means a river, something that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the huge river flowing through Brazil and to the online shopping giant famous for home deliveries.

clue.text: Quibble with Balkan city hotel over pretentious behaviour

parts.note: Split is a port city in Croatia
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
putting on airs is behaving pretentiously

explanation.surface: A guest grumbles about a Balkan hotel's snooty staff.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts the hotel letter above the airs; the Croatian city name is the first half of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To split hairs is an idiom for arguing over trivial distinctions, which is exactly what quibbling means.

clue.text: Chelsea at the top, with passion play away

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the club's name
heat is intensity of feeling, as in the heat of the moment

explanation.surface: Chelsea top the table and play their away fixture with real passion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play away' sounds like football, matching Chelsea, but it is British slang for being unfaithful to a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: To play away is an informal idiom for having an affair, and to cheat on someone is the same infidelity.

clue.text: Ofcom mendaciously suppressing acclaim

indicators.note: to suppress something is to keep it held down inside, so the words hold the answer within them

parts.note: runs across the end of the regulator's name and the start of the adverb

explanation.surface: The broadcasting regulator dishonestly stifles praise for a programme.
explanation.walkthrough: Ofcom is the UK's broadcasting and communications regulator; the answer straddles the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To commend is to praise publicly, which is what acclaiming does; both are verbs of approval.

clue.text: Fair cop to begin with, restricting Yankee's licence

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so one piece surrounds another
this phrase sets the order, putting the named piece at the front of the line

parts.note: taken as written
fair and right both mean just or proper
Y is Yankee in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An arrested American admits it's a fair cop while the police check his licence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a fair cop' is what a caught criminal traditionally says, but here the two words are separate pieces, with the policeman going first.
explanation.definitionFit: Copyright is the legal right to reproduce a work, and permission granted under it is a form of licence.

clue.text: I'm not sure interrupting the setter is trivial

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: the setter refers to himself as me
er is the hesitant sound of uncertainty

explanation.surface: Someone hesitantly cuts in to tell the compiler his work is lightweight.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves as 'the setter' or 'this compiler', which gives a first-person pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Mere means small or insignificant, as in a mere trifle, so it matches trivial as an adjective.

clue.text: Grace Kelly's second stage frolic, not the first

indicators.note: this tells us to drop the opening letter from the word it follows
second points to the letter in position two of the name

parts.note: the second letter of the surname
a leg is a stage of a journey or race
to dance is to frolic or caper

explanation.surface: Film star Grace Kelly's second big role, in a playful romp on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Grace Kelly reads as one name, but 'Grace' is the definition and only Kelly's second letter is used; DANCE loses its D.
explanation.definitionFit: Grace and elegance are synonyms for refined, beautiful poise in movement or manner.

clue.text: Wastes oysters prepared day before

indicators.note: before sets the order, putting one piece ahead of the other

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for day

indicators.note: food that is prepared has been worked over and rearranged, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Oysters shucked a day ahead are spoiled and thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' places D ahead of the rearranged shellfish, even though it comes last in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To waste something can mean to ruin or lay it waste, so wastes and destroys are matching verbs.

clue.text: Will occasionally pursuing a tax cut help?

indicators.note: cutting something trims off its end, so the last letter goes
to pursue is to come after, so this piece follows the other

parts.note: taken as written
VAT is value added tax, the UK sales tax

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the name

explanation.surface: Would a small tax cut ever be any help?
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is the UK's value added tax, the standard tax in crosswords; 'Will' looks like a name or the future tense but is only a letter source.
explanation.definitionFit: Avail as a noun means use or benefit, as in to no avail, matching help in a question.

clue.text: Old doormen could become dealers

parts.note: ex means former
porters guard the doors of buildings and colleges

explanation.surface: Retired doormen might take up a new career in trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could become' sounds like an anagram signal but simply joins the wordplay to the definition here.
explanation.definitionFit: Exporters are traders who sell goods abroad, so they are dealers in a commercial sense.

clue.text: Anecdote from Rishi Sunak perhaps taking seconds

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece is absorbed inside another

parts.note: the former Conservative prime minister, who is not tall, is an example of a small member of the party
S is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A tale told by the former prime minister while helping himself to second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishi Sunak, a Tory (Conservative) prime minister, is noted for his modest height; 'perhaps' marks him as one example of the description.
explanation.definitionFit: An anecdote is a brief narrative, and a short story is a compact piece of fiction; loosely the same thing.

clue.text: Match piano with song

parts.note: p is the musical marking for piano, softly
an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: Choose the right piano accompaniment for a song.
explanation.walkthrough: Both musical words are pieces, and 'Match' is the verb being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: To pair things is to put them together as a couple, which is what matching them means.

clue.text: Family cleans up completely in violent events

parts.note: blood means kin, as in blood relatives
a person who baths washes all over

explanation.surface: A household scrubs up thoroughly after something nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English 'bath' is also a verb, to wash someone in a bath.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloodbath is a massacre or scene of great carnage, so the plural names violent events.

clue.text: Carefree naked chaps — gutsy, filled with variable energy

indicators.note: naked means stripped of covering, so the outer letters are removed
something filled has contents placed inside it, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: the word with its first and last letters stripped
plucky means brave and spirited
y is a standard algebraic variable
go means vigour or energy

explanation.surface: Naked lads, feeling brave and full of fluctuating vigour, run about without a care.
explanation.walkthrough: In algebra x, y and z are the usual variables, and 'go' as a noun means get-up-and-go; both slip into the brave word just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Happy-go-lucky describes someone cheerfully unconcerned about the future, the same easy-going outlook as carefree.

clue.text: Rich fudge upset Leon

indicators.note: to fudge is to fiddle or fake, so the letters are manipulated into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Too much rich sweet fudge has given poor Leon a bad stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fudge' looks like the sweet and 'upset' looks like the anagram signal; in fact 'fudge' is the signal and 'upset' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenteous is a literary word for abundant or plentiful, which is one sense of rich, as in rich harvest.

clue.text: Set focus for City and United in full

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the following word

parts.note: sated means having eaten one's fill

indicators.note: a focus is a central point, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of the word
U is the abbreviation for United in team names

explanation.surface: A football pundit wants the fans of two Manchester clubs to concentrate.
explanation.walkthrough: City and United are the two Manchester football clubs, but here they are only letter sources, placed inside a word meaning well fed.
explanation.definitionFit: Set can mean placed or located, as in a house set on a hill, which is what situated means.

clue.text: Show on TV casually or precisely

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the everyday shortened name of a popular BBC celebrity ballroom contest
second meaning: exactly, in a rigorous sense

explanation.walkthrough: Strictly Come Dancing is a popular BBC celebrity ballroom show, usually just called by its first word; 'casually' marks that shortening.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means exactly or in the narrowest sense, as in strictly speaking, and it is also the show's nickname.

clue.text: Involvement of the heartless Republican in lie

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the following word

parts.note: an invention is a fabrication or untruth

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle is gone, so only the outer letters remain

parts.note: the word with its middle letter removed
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A cold-hearted American politician is caught up in a falsehood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The heartless Republican' reads as a political jibe, but 'heartless' only strips the middle letter from 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Intervention is getting involved in a situation to change its course, so it is a kind of involvement.

clue.text: Avert getting confused by latest of tickets — go without fare

indicators.note: by means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side
the latest of anything is its final one, so only the end letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

indicators.note: confused things are jumbled, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A confused traveller without a ticket skips the fare and goes without.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' suggests a bus or train ticket price, matching 'tickets', but here it means food.
explanation.definitionFit: Fare also means food, so to go without fare is to go hungry, which is to starve.

clue.text: Propose a date when king heads away

parts.note: as can mean when, as in as I left
K is king in chess notation
someone out is away from home

explanation.surface: A courtier suggests a day for the meeting once the monarch has left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Propose a date' reads like fixing an appointment for the king, but a date here is a romantic outing.
explanation.definitionFit: To ask someone out is the idiom for inviting them on a romantic outing, so it proposes a date.

clue.text: Company's in the dark, 50 dismissed

indicators.note: someone dismissed is sent away, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: a place in the dark has no lights on
L is fifty in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A firm keeps its staff uninformed after laying off fifty workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the dark' suggests being uninformed, but it is read literally as unlit.
explanation.definitionFit: A company is a military body of soldiers, and a unit is any such organised group within an army.

clue.text: Properties American, given time, compliments

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
T is the abbreviation for time
tributes are expressions of praise

explanation.surface: An American estate agent, given a moment, praises the houses on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Properties' looks like real estate, which suits the American salesman, but it means qualities.
explanation.definitionFit: Properties in the sense of characteristic qualities are attributes, features belonging to something.

clue.text: Fish under river's rocks

indicators.note: in a down clue, being under puts one piece below the other in the column

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for river
eels are long snake-like fish

explanation.surface: Fish lurk beneath the stones of a river bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocks' looks like a noun for stones in the river; it is the verb meaning sways.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that reels staggers or sways unsteadily, just as something that rocks moves to and fro.

clue.text: Trotters making Del's heart sink in outdoor function

indicators.note: to sink is to drop down, so that letter leaves its place and falls to the bottom of the column

parts.note: trotters are pigs' feet, used jokingly for anyone's

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter

parts.note: the middle letter of the name

explanation.surface: The Trotter family of the sitcom Only Fools and Horses, with Del Boy dejected at a village event.
explanation.walkthrough: Del Boy Trotter is the hero of the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses. The E (centre of Del) moves from second place down to the bottom of the column.
explanation.definitionFit: A fete is an outdoor fair or festival with stalls and games, typically held to raise money.

clue.text: Possibly lead championship list when announced

parts.note: a title is a championship won in sport

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so we go by the sound rather than the spelling

parts.note: a roll is a list of names

explanation.surface: A sports team may top the championship table when results are read out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like leading a league, but it means the star part in a play; 'possibly' warns that this is only one kind.
explanation.definitionFit: The title role is the part named in a play's title, such as Hamlet, which is usually but not always the lead.

clue.text: Body temperature, approximately

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for temperature
or so means roughly, as in ten or so

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a vague reading on a thermometer; the definition comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: The torso is the trunk of the human frame, the main part apart from head and limbs, so a body.

clue.text: Cutting head leads to desire for a drink

parts.note: a cutting or dry remark is sharply ironic
a ness is a headland, common in British place names like Sheerness

explanation.surface: A hairdresser's snipping makes the customer thirsty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting head' looks like a haircut or beheading; the words are separate pieces, and 'leads to' only joins them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryness of the mouth and throat is thirst, the sensation of needing liquid refreshment.

clue.text: Feel dodgy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a verb, to have a hunch that something is so
second meaning: an adjective, of doubtful honesty or reliability

explanation.walkthrough: Two words that read as one phrase about feeling unwell are separate senses of one word, said with different stresses.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to believe or sense something without proof; as an adjective it means questionable or untrustworthy.
